title: Comparative Analysis of Tracheal Intubation-Associated Cardiac Arrest in 2015-2023: A Report From the National Emergency Airway Registry for Children Multicenter Registry
summary: This retrospective cohort used prospectively collected NEAR4KIDS registry data from 27,773 initial tracheal intubations in pediatric and pediatric cardiac ICUs from 2015 through 2023. Tracheal intubation-associated cardiac arrest occurred in 331 intubations (1.2%). Pre-intubation oxygenation failure and shock were associated with higher arrest odds, and each additional intubation attempt was associated with progressively higher risk; video laryngoscopy, neuromuscular blockade, ketamine, and propofol were associated with lower odds in adjusted analyses.
findings: Tracheal intubation-associated cardiac arrest occurred in 331 of 27,773 intubations (1.2%).
Pre-intubation oxygenation failure and shock were associated with higher odds of intubation-associated cardiac arrest.
Each additional tracheal intubation attempt was associated with higher arrest odds.
Ketamine, propofol, neuromuscular blockade, and video laryngoscopy were associated with lower adjusted odds; these observational associations do not establish causality.
comparator: Intubations without tracheal intubation-associated cardiac arrest.
population: Critically ill children undergoing initial tracheal intubation in pediatric ICUs and pediatric cardiac ICUs participating in the international NEAR4KIDS registry.
shortTitle: Pediatric intubation-associated cardiac arrest: modifiable risk signals
limitations: This was an observational PICU/PCICU registry study rather than an ED randomized trial, so residual confounding and setting-specific practice are important. Associations involving induction drugs, neuromuscular blockade, and video laryngoscopy do not prove those choices prevent arrest.
intervention: Tracheal intubation characteristics and peri-intubation practices; no randomized intervention.
whyItMatters: The modifiable signal is procedural and physiologic: optimize oxygenation and hemodynamics before pediatric intubation and prioritize first-attempt success. The medication and device associations are hypothesis-generating and should not be converted into causal ED protocol changes from this registry study alone.
evidenceNotes: Primary journal abstract and PubMed record reviewed. The study used prospectively collected registry data but a retrospective observational analysis; medication and device associations require cautious interpretation.
primaryEndpoint: Tracheal intubation-associated cardiac arrest, defined as cardiac arrest or chest compressions temporally associated with intubation.
